item.title: GDOL extends In-School Youth Program application deadline to Oct. 30
item.description: The Guam Department of Labor and Guam Community College have extended the application deadline for the In-School Youth Year-Round Program to Oct. 30, following disruptions caused by Typhoon Champi. The previous deadline was Oct. 24. The extension gives students and families additional time to complete and submit applications.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Department of Labor and Guam Community College have extended the application deadline for the In-School Youth Year-Round Program to Oct. 30, following disruptions caused by Typhoon Champi.

The previous deadline was Oct. 24. The extension gives students and families additional time to complete and submit applications.

The program offers eligible 11th-grade students professional development, communications, customer service, and leadership training, along with paid employment opportunities. It has also expanded to include students enrolled in GCC’s Career and Technical Education program.

Participants take part in a two-week winter session and a one-week spring session before completing six weeks of paid summer employment with private-sector employers in fields or industries that interest them. All sessions provide a stipend.

To qualify, students must be in the 11th grade or be part of the GCC Career and Technical Education program and meet other program eligibility requirements.

Interested students can apply online at bit.ly/inschoolyouth or contact their school counselor for more information.

For assistance, contact the American Job Center at 671-475-7500 or email ajc.training@dol.guam.gov . Additional information about the department’s youth program is available at dol.guam.gov .

item.title: Breaking Wave Theatre redirects show proceeds to Typhoon Champi recovery
item.description: Breaking Wave Theatre Company is redirecting proceeds from its upcoming live tabletop adventure show to support local recovery efforts following Typhoon Champi. The nonprofit will host “Tides of Fantasy: The House with Teeth” from 6:30 to 10:30 p.m. Saturday at its headquarters in the MTM Building in Momong-Toto-Maite.
item.content:encoded:
Breaking Wave Theatre Company is redirecting proceeds from its upcoming live tabletop adventure show to support local recovery efforts following Typhoon Champi.

The nonprofit will host “Tides of Fantasy: The House with Teeth” from 6:30 to 10:30 p.m. Saturday at its headquarters in the MTM Building in Momong-Toto-Maite.

Originally planned as a fundraiser for the company’s year-round arts programming, the focus shifted after members volunteered with World Central Kitchen and witnessed the needs of families affected by the storm.

The company has also replaced its original $50 admission price with pay-what-you-can tickets ranging from $10 to $50. All ticket levels provide the same experience. Those facing financial barriers to attending can contact events@bwtcguam.com . Individuals and businesses interested in sponsoring tickets for others may also reach out to the organization.

The live tabletop roleplaying show will feature a group of adventurers building a fantasy story through improvisation, character decisions, and dice rolls guided by Game Master James Aevermann.

The event is intended for audiences ages 18 and older. Tickets are available through Guam Time Events.

item.title: CNMI governor seeks revenue sharing, safeguards in seabed mining proposal
item.description: Gov. David M. Apatang said the Commonwealth supports national efforts to secure critical mineral supplies but urged federal officials to address a wide range of environmental, economic and cultural concerns before advancing a proposed offshore mineral lease sale near the Northern Mariana Islands. In comments submitted Oct. 16 to the U.S. Dept. of the Interior and its Marine Minerals Administration
item.content:encoded:
Gov. David M. Apatang said the Commonwealth supports national efforts to secure critical mineral supplies but urged federal officials to address a wide range of environmental, economic and cultural concerns before advancing a proposed offshore mineral lease sale near the Northern Mariana Islands.

In comments submitted Oct. 16 to the U.S. Dept. of the Interior and its Marine Minerals Administration, Apatang said he recognizes and supports President Donald Trump's goal of reducing U.S. dependence on foreign sources of critical minerals used in technology, clean energy, transportation, health care and defense industries. However, he said national supply-chain objectives should not outweigh potential impacts on CNMI residents and the marine environment.

"The CNMI cannot evaluate the proposed lease sale solely on the basis of national mineral supply chain security objectives and dominance," Apatang wrote, adding that any decision should balance national interests with the well-being of CNMI residents and marine ecosystems.

The governor's comments were submitted in response to the proposed leasing notice for Pacific Minerals Lease Sale 2, or PACM-2, which would make portions of the Outer Continental Shelf around the CNMI available for critical mineral exploration and development.

Apatang noted that more than 65,000 public comments were submitted during an earlier federal information-gathering process and said all should be considered, particularly those expressing concerns about potential environmental harm from deep-sea mining. He said residents have voiced strong opposition to offshore mining and emphasized the longstanding cultural and personal connection indigenous island communities have with the ocean.

The governor also encouraged federal officials to pause the leasing process until two pending federal court cases in Hawaii have been resolved, arguing that proceeding before judicial review is completed could prove inefficient and costly.

In an 11-page letter, Apatang outlined numerous questions and recommendations for federal officials, including whether the CNMI would receive a share of lease revenues and what economic benefits would flow to the Commonwealth if mining activities move forward. He also called for enforceable commitments on local hiring, procurement, workforce development, and infrastructure investments.

The governor further requested additional environmental baseline studies addressing deep-sea coral communities, seamount ecosystems, fisheries, marine mammals, sediment plumes, underwater noise and other potential impacts. He proposed creating a CNMI Marine Minerals Environmental Monitoring Program funded by leaseholders.

Among other recommendations, Apatang sought fisheries compensation mechanisms, protections for cultural and traditional resources, stronger financial assurance requirements, emergency-response funding, safeguards against excessive concentration of lease ownership and restrictions on foreign control of strategically important mineral resources.

He also asked federal officials to clarify how offshore mineral activities would be coordinated with military operations in the Mariana Islands Range Complex and requested a formal framework for continued CNMI participation in future review and permitting processes.

Apatang said the CNMI remains willing to work with federal agencies to identify what he described as a responsible path forward, but stressed that residents should not bear disproportionate environmental, economic or infrastructure-related costs associated with offshore mineral development. He acknowledged that many residents favor a more direct alternative.

"The alternative, as voiced by many CNMI residents, is no mining at all," Apatang wrote

item.title: Actor Tom Skerritt, who played dads, cops and commanding officers, has died
item.description: There's no avoiding the word rugged with Tom Skerritt. There was the mustache, the jaw, the crinkly eyes, and the cool authoritarian bearing he brought to memorable roles as commanding officers, dads and cops. Skerritt died of natural causes on Wednesday, according to a statement from a representative. He was 93 years old.
item.content:encoded:
There's no avoiding the word rugged with Tom Skerritt. There was the mustache, the jaw, the crinkly eyes, and the cool authoritarian bearing he brought to memorable roles as commanding officers, dads and cops.

Skerritt died of natural causes on Wednesday, according to a statement from a representative. He was 93 years old.

He was Captain Dallas in Alien . Viper in Top Gun . An enlistee in the original movie M*A*S*H ( playing one of the few characters who didn't transition to the later television series.) A Vietnam vet in the Cheech and Chong stoner classic, Up In Smoke . He played small town sheriffs in the movie The Dead Zone and on the TV series Picket Fences , for which he won an Emmy in 1993.

And he was a dad in Ice Castles, Steel Magnolias and A River Runs Through It .

Skerritt described himself as a blue-collar kid from Detroit who served in the Air Force before attending UCLA and turning to theater. He spent his early days in Hollywood appearing in television shows, from My Three Sons to The Alfred Hitchcock Hour , and hanging out with the likes of Robert Redford and director Hal Ashby, who cast Skerritt in Harold and Maude (as a cop, of course).

In real life, Skerritt promoted independent film and theater in the Pacific Northwest, where he lived. He co-founded The Red Badge Project, a program for veterans to take storytelling courses and share their experiences.

item.title: Federal judge restricts DHS field operations looking for noncitizen voters
item.description: A federal judge in California is putting limits on pre-election field operations conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that the agency says is aimed at trying to find noncitizens who have illegally voted in nine states. item.content:encoded:
A federal judge in California is putting limits on pre-election field operations conducted by the Department of Homeland Security that the agency says is aimed at trying to find noncitizens who have illegally voted in nine states.

In recent weeks, armed Homeland Security Investigations officers have carried out field operations and visited homes to interview people suspected of illegally voting as noncitizens. The targets can include people who became citizens but voted before they naturalized.

In a 19-page order late Wednesday, U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín, an appointee of President Joe Biden, wrote that the federal government was using "flawed" data in the initiative and that its efforts likely violated the Voting Rights Act, which bars voter intimidation.

Martínez-Olguín referenced a disclosure last month from a U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services whistleblower that alleged rushed efforts to match data to create a target list of potential noncitizens on voter rolls, and that the list includes U.S. citizens. She also pointed to HSI's social media posts, including one that showed agents handcuffing a California man accused of unlawfully registering to vote.

The judge wrote that the government's use of unreliable and incomplete data along with highly publicized arrests "lead to an objectively reasonable fear of law enforcement entanglements that intimidates citizens from urging or aiding others in exercising their right to vote."

HSI field operations were planned in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin, according to documents produced in the case and CNN reporting .

Martínez-Olguín barred DHS officers in those states from conducting field operations targeting people they "know, suspect, or should reasonably know or suspect are U.S. citizens," or that are based "wholly" on USCIS matching data without further investigation.

In a declaration , USCIS official Nicolas Bartell had told the judge his team manually reviews records before referring them to HSI, but acknowledged the "low possibility" citizens could be "erroneously identified as potential aliens" in federal records. He wrote the risks were mitigated by safeguards his office takes "and any remaining risks were outweighed by the need to support the agency's law-enforcement and election-integrity mission."

It's unclear how much of an effect the judge's order will have on the federal government's highly publicized campaign to find noncitizen voters.

States reviews and audits have consistently found voting by noncitizens to be extremely rare .

"DHS is laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of U.S. citizens. ONLY Americans should elect American leaders," the agency wrote in a statement. "We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens."

The order is set to take effect on Friday and would be in effect through election night, though the federal government could appeal.

The judge's ruling came in a lawsuit filed last month by a coalition that includes San Francisco and Santa Clara counties, the city of San Francisco, nursing unions and Voto Latino Foundation. Protect Democracy and the National Immigration Law Center are litigating the case against the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice.

"Today, the courts affirmed a vital principle of our democracy: Voting is a fundamental right that citizens — whether born here or naturalized — should be able to exercise without armed government agents harassing them," Beau Tremitiere, a lawyer with Protect Democracy, said in a statement.

"It was clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people's homes weeks before an election," he added.

A court filing by the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United described naturalized citizen members who no longer wanted to attend political rallies, sign up to be election poll workers, or vote in person because of the federal operations.

The order comes as the Department of Justice is suing California and demanding the state segregate 20,000 ballots from people federal officials say they believe are "likely" noncitizens.

A preliminary review of a sample of that list by Los Angeles County election officials found many of the registrations were canceled, inactive or had no voting history, and some pertained to people who indicated they were born in the U.S.

The DOJ announced charges against 28 green card holders across the state on Monday who are accused of illegally voting or registering to vote.

item.title: Betty Gilpin seeks out 'anti-algorithm' projects, like 'The Lowdown' and 'Widow's Bay'

item.content:encoded:
In more than 20 years of acting, Betty Gilpin's roles have fit into a variety of tropes, including "femme fatales and calming wives and evil mistresses." But recently she's been offered a wider range of opportunities.

"One of the many benefits of aging is that you sort of age out of being an archetype, like your id sort of seeps through — whether you like it or not. ... I was really struck by how much I look like myself," she says of her current role starring opposite Ethan Hawke in Season 2 of the FX noir series The Lowdown.

Gilpin's character on The Lowdown is a public defender who asks for help from Hawke's character, the self-appointed investigative journalist. Last month, she won an Emmy Award for her guest performance in the Apple TV series, Widow's Bay , a horror-comedy about an island community that may actually be cursed. Her character was a woman living in the early 1700s, whose story was a vital part of the island's dark history.

"I feel like there are many parallels between Widow's Bay and Lowdown [in] that they're so sort of anti-algorithm," Gilpin says. "There's an understandable pull in my industry to make things that are kind of like a gleaming vanilla car commercial, like super safe, super familiar, appeal to the masses. ... And [then there are] people that are out there who are like, I'm actually going to go the other way and make something so inexplicable and strange ... and weird and unrecognizable."

In 2024, Gilpin brought her brand of weird to Oh, Mary! , Cole Escola 's Broadway farce about the former first lady Mary Todd Lincoln — a role she compares to giving a yorkie terrier cocaine and then telling the dog to "go on as Hamlet's understudy inside the Coliseum."

"There's so many jobs that feel like you're being asked to do 5% of what you can do and that can be really, really hard and sad. And then [with] Mary Todd in Cole's play, you're being asked to do 105% of what you can do," she says.

Gilpin's breakthrough role was on the Netflix series, GLOW , which earned her three Emmy nominations. Her current films include Office Romance and The Social Reckoning . She's also the author of a collection of essays called All the Women in My Brain: And Other Concerns.

On winning an Emmy Award for her guest performance on Widow's Bay

I feel a little embarrassed that that's my Emmy because I worked for seven days on it. I know that, like, people who make TV shows, it's a years-long, extremely difficult, arduous process where people fry their personal lives and brains and sob through notes and forget to book doctor's appointments for themselves because they are working all hours, making this possible. And then I came in and memorized some lines and crossed my eyes and left and I got a trophy. ...

I feel very lucky that it's happened now and not 10, 15 years ago. I think while I'm so happy and excited and feel so lucky, there was not one cell in me that was like, "Yes, finally!" It was just a really nice night. And then I was excited to go home to my daughters.

My dad [played] sort of stern lawyer-types — butlers, lawyers, and, like, a reliable, smart man who knew the way. My mom is just farce incarnate. She's the funniest person on Earth. So much of my Oh, Mary! performance is just plagiarism from [my mother] Ann McDonough. ...

I think [there was] an Agatha Christie play where she was a maid and — it was certainly not in the script — she just had to exit and she made a choice where she just slowly pulled up her dress so you could see her knees and she's sort of, like, pointed her pelvis towards her male scene partner and kind of reverse crab walked away from him in a weird, haunted, sultry, farcical maid way. And it brought the house down in a not-comedy. People couldn't breathe, they were laughing so hard. ...

It was a profound and strange way to grow up. I saw my parents put themselves in many different people's shoes, and it expands the possibility of your life and makes you curious about the different lives that your parents have and that you could have, and I wanted to have all of them — and now I'm addicted to it.

On how she replaced Cole Escola in Oh, Mary!

[It was] a total insane fluke of the timeline of the world. Cole and I had never met, but they followed me on Instagram. I have a private Instagram. And it's me in my trailer, basically, in various jobs in my career, in various crazy costumes. And I'm pretending that I am a sort of half Blanche Dubois , half Valerie Cherish from The Comeback ... a regional theater actress losing her mind in her dressing room at half hour before some play that she's about to do. And I guess Cole thought, well, she may just be demented enough to replace me in Oh, Mary! , to be the guinea pig to see if it would work without Cole. They offered me the part. It was so insane that day getting that call, and it was the experience of my life.

On why she's been in so many period pieces

I can probably credit my mom's whimsy and dad's diction. And I went to theater school where we trained for four years and were told, like, get ready for all the Shakespeare parts! And my experience was I graduated and it was the era of the pixie dream girl . I think often my training and gravitas or ... palpable self-loathing and pain in my eyes translates to oldie-timey?

On her first TV role, in which she played a dead body on Law & Order

It was my honor to be a dead body. I did have one alive line. I was Fran Drescher 's daughter, but then I got a gunshot to the neck pretty quickly. … The guy who kills me is Shane McRae, who is in this season of The Lowdown . It can feel like being an actor is a series of controlled connections. Like your job is to hyper-connect with people and then say goodbye to them. Now, having done this for 21 years, it feels like I have cousins all over, well, maybe not cousins — cousins with sexual tension and shared trauma — all over this industry, and it feels so wonderful. It's such a privilege.

On how her role in the wrestling drama GLOW changed her relationship to her body

It was really the first time I thought about my body being a functional, powerful thing. And it completely changed the way I thought about approaching a part, that it could be a head-to-toe thing, versus a neck-up thing. I had an acting teacher once tell me that I was "a good actor from the neck up and scared Betty from the shoulders down" — and he was right on. I just felt so disconnected from my body. Not that that's all fixed now, but wrestling really helped, just to be as simultaneously stupid and powerful as possible.

I had assigned it in my mind that wrestling was all about macho and hyper masculine and these guys must have huge egos. ... [But] it's all about vulnerability. It's not gonna look real unless you make your partner look like the strongest person who's ever touched you. That's what makes a good actor, that they understand that the best version of something is finding music between you versus you looking like the coolest poster possible. Wrestling felt like kind of this meta exercise of reminder that our job is to take care of each other in these scenes and to find it together.

Lauren Krenzel and Susan Nyakundi produced and edited this interview for broadcast. Bridget Bentz, Molly Seavy-Nesper and Beth Novey adapted it for the web.

item.title: You're invited to a party at Duke Ellington's house in 'Once Upon a Time in Harlem'
item.description: We spend our lives swimming in an ocean of footage. item.content:encoded:
We spend our lives swimming in an ocean of footage. Crimes, meals, ugly cats, parachute jumps, public rudeness, private sex — seemingly everything is now recorded and shared with the world. It wasn't always so. It's a thrill when someone uncovers footage of great people from the past whose achievements feel almost mythological.

This is part of the magic of Once Upon a Time in Harlem , a new documentary that had its beginnings in 1972, when filmmaker William Greaves hosted a cocktail party at Duke Ellington 's townhouse. As his guests, he invited the surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance, the blossoming of artistic and intellectual life that took off after World War I and flowered into the mid-1930s.

Greaves filmed the occasion, but never made it into a finished movie. Half a century later, his son David — one of the cameramen at the party — took that footage and completed the job. The result is a wonder, like watching a 50th college reunion set on Mt. Olympus.

Here is a party packed with legends, some born not long after the Civil War, nearly all blessed with a sense of style. They range from 85-year-old musician Eubie Blake and painter Aaron Douglas — known as the father of African-American art — to poet Arna Bontemps and photographer James Van Der Zee, whose gorgeous black–and-white stills are interspersed throughout. It's an imposing crew. As Blake jokes, "To be here with all these intelligentsias, I'm afraid to open my mouth."

Greaves' camera follows his guests as they mingle and drink, capturing eddies of chitchat filled with terrific stories, personal preening, and jokes about Marcus Garvey . Artist Romare Bearden boasts that his new book is becoming a bestseller; Ida Mae Cullen frets that her late husband, the poet Countee Cullen, is being neglected. Even as actor Leigh Whipper, 96, talks about working in minstrel shows, the elegant society editor Gerri Major recalls being spat on by a white patron at the Cotton Club.

David Greaves and his editors give all this talk unobtrusively nifty themes and echoes. For instance, Blake says that, contrary to popular opinion, it's not true that he won't shake hands with a white man. He just won't extend his hand first. Later, we hear a story of how Bill "Bojangles" Robinson stuck out his hand to shake with Charles Lindbergh after his famous flight, only to have the racist aviator turn away from him. And this gets its payoff when Bearden points out that the greatest artistic tribute to Lindbergh was none other than the Lindy Hop , a dance created ... in Harlem. To music, I would add, by Eubie Blake .

Langston Hughes , who died before this party, was a leading light of the Renaissance, and preached — as Arna Bontemps tells us — that Black artists should claim a new freedom. Greaves himself was born in Harlem in the late '20s and dreamed of being an actor — even studying the Method alongside Marlon Brando . But realizing that Black actors wouldn't get good roles, he turned to making documentaries, and directed scores of films during the Civil Rights era that captured the lives of actual Black people who were vastly more diverse and interesting than the fictional ones on stage and screen.

You feel his sensitive touch in Once Upon a Time in Harlem , whose guests are no monolithic troupe of geriatrics. These are sharp individuals of great distinction, with the big egos and big opinions that come with that. They still argue, sometimes angrily, over 1920s questions that remain vexing in the 2020s. Should Black artists see themselves as Black Artists or American Artists or just artists? Should Black thinkers tell the truth as they see it, or try to promote the race? "If I can't do something that's going to help us," the journalist Major says, "I'm not going to do something that's going to hurt us."

The film is rich with inspiring sections, from its discussion of the importance of women to the Renaissance — Zora Neale Hurston 's dazzling brilliance is duly celebrated — to moments when you feel the valiant souls of those we're watching. Few things are more stirring than seeing activist Richard B. Moore, who initially comes off a bit cold, spontaneously recite by heart Claude McKay's sonnet, "If We Must Die," a poem that ends:

Early in the film, we hear from Regina Andrews, a librarian who helped encourage and promote the Harlem Renaissance. She says of that legendary time, "It was hard not to be caught up. You got pulled along in a way. You just couldn't stop yourself." Watching Once Upon a Time in Harlem , I got pulled along, too.
